description_full: RELX PLC, together with its subsidiaries, provides information-based analytics and decision tools for professional and business customers in North America, Europe, and internationally. It operates through four segments: Risk; Scientific, Technical & Medical; Legal; and Exhibitions. The Risk segment offers information-based analytics and decision tools that combine public and industry specific content with technology and algorithms to assist clients in evaluating and predicting risk, as well as a portfolio of commercial healthcare products. Its Scientific, Technical & Medical segment provides scientific and medical information and data sets for science and healthcare. The Legal segment provides legal, regulatory, and business information and analytics. Its Exhibitions segment combines digital tools and data to help customers connect in-person and online, discover new markets, source products, generate leads, and transact. The company was formerly known as Reed Elsevier PLC and changed its name to RELX PLC in July 2015. RELX PLC was incorporated in 1903 and is headquartered in London, the United Kingdom.

financial_summary: RELX PLC PLC is a large-cap industrials business with a $69.7B market cap on $12.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 21% against a 8% cost of capital — a 14-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 65% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $3.8B in free cash flow — roughly 29 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.36× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 10.2×.

Shareholder yield of 2.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
